name: Furosemide for hollow cheeks

lead: Some looksmax.org users take furosemide (Lasix), a prescription loop diuretic, to reduce water retention and facial puffiness. The aim is a more defined, hollower-looking cheek and jawline, often timed before an event. Posters call it the hollow cheek pill.

Furosemide works by increasing salt and water loss in urine, with effects generally beginning within an hour or so. Any change in the face reflects temporary fluid loss rather than a change in fat or bone. Published literature concerns its medical uses, not cosmetic ones.

paras: Forum guides describe it as taken ahead of an occasion, typically with attention to salt and fluid intake, and note that effects appear within a couple of hours [1]. It is a prescription medicine obtained through a clinician in the US, UK, EU and Australia [2].

Documented adverse effects include low blood pressure, electrolyte disturbance (especially low potassium), dehydration that can stress the kidneys, tinnitus and hearing loss, and photosensitivity [2]. Using diuretics for appearance is not an approved use, and the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits furosemide in sport [2].

angle.text: The practice aims at a short-term cosmetic effect: reducing water held in the face so contours look sharper. Users describe it as an event-day measure rather than a lasting change.

lead: Furosemide for hollow cheeks is a practice on looksmax.org in which people take furosemide, sold as Lasix and under other names, to reduce water retention for a leaner-looking face. Users call it the hollow cheek pill and describe the effect as less facial puffiness and sharper cheek and jaw definition within a few hours [1].

Furosemide is a loop diuretic approved for edema from heart failure, liver or kidney disease and for high blood pressure; oral doses start working in about 30 to 60 minutes [2]. The cosmetic use is an off-label forum practice, and no published trial has examined it for facial appearance.

Its temporary effect comes from fluid loss, so users describe timing it for photos or nights out [1]. Medical sources list dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities and low blood pressure among its risks [2].
infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, EU, Australia [2]

paras: Forum guides present furosemide as a quick debloating tool, with debloating said to occur within roughly two hours [1]. The guide's author describes advance planning, such as limiting high-sodium foods beforehand, and disputes advice to drink large volumes of water because the drug removes water [1]. This article does not reproduce dosing or sourcing details.

The author of the main looksmax.org guide says interest increased in recent months and that they had written multiple earlier threads on the topic [1]. Furosemide has a long history as a drug used by athletes and bodybuilders to drop water weight, which is why it is on WADA's prohibited list as a masking agent [2].

Furosemide blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop of Henle, so more sodium, chloride and potassium leave in urine and water follows [2]. Diuresis usually finishes within six to eight hours of an oral dose [2].

Clinical references list orthostatic hypotension, tinnitus, photosensitivity, low potassium and other electrolyte abnormalities, gout, raised blood sugar, and hearing loss among adverse effects. Excess fluid loss can cause dehydration and temporary kidney injury [2]. It is a prescription-only drug in the US, UK, EU and Australia [2].
No studies found. Published studies of furosemide concern its approved medical uses, not facial appearance.
